newsitem.title: UK: UK Budget -- Round-up of day-after analyst comment.
newsitem.headline: UK Budget -- Round-up of day-after analyst comment.

text.p: Following is a round-up of analyst comment on the 1997/98 UK budget presented by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday:
MICHAEL SAUNDERS, SALOMON BROTHERS:

The budget maintains the cautious approach of the last few years. In our view...a reasonable judgement is that the budget is slightly tight. The budget, on top of the existing tough baseline plans, will tighten the overall fiscal stance by about 0.7 percent of GDP in 1997/98, similar to this year.
Fiscal caution will limit the upward pressure on base rates...

The budget probably is not tight enough to rule out further rate hikes but counts against a very big rate hike. With buoyant growth and above-target inflation, we suspect that base rates will rise by 0.75 percent to 6.75 percent by mid-1997. The odds on a December hike are about 50:50.

As markets digest the budget, we expect the gilt-Bund spread to fall to about 160 basis points in coming weeks...The budget should help to dispel the view that the UK is a fiscal laggard. The UK's fiscal numbers in 1997 will be similar to the EU norm: sizeable fiscal tightening and a deficit of about three percent of GDP. Moreover the budget has a longer-term significance.

If fiscal orthodoxy prevails in the current position, with the government well down in the polls and facing a near-term election, then risks of future slippage are probably less than markets price in.

The budget in itself is probably neutral for sterling. The potential boost from evidence of continued policy orthodoxy is likely to be offset by lower expectations for the path of base rates in 1997. At current levels, sterling is no longer significantly undervalued.

There may still be scope for a modest further gain because of the upward pressure to real short rates from the forthcoming consumer windfalls and favourable current account trends. We expect sterling to edge up to about DM 2.60 in the next year.
JAMES BARTY, CIARAN BARR AND STEVEN BELL, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL

Clarke...announced a small rise in taxes, a mild overall fiscal contraction and a complete absence of radical measures. This raises the question of why Mr Clarke decided not to deliver a populist budget and take the risk of upsetting the financial markets.
The answer is that he firmly believes thet "doing the right thing" is good politics as well as good economics.

By framing a neutral/tight budget, Clarke may be hoping that he can avoid having to raise rates again before the election. If this softens sterling, he would see this as an additional advantage...Mr Clarke has decided that a "do nothing" budget maximises his party's chances of a fifth successive electoral victory. He may be right but the odds still suggest that the next budget will be delivered by Mr Gordon Brown of the Labour party.

We believe the Chancellor will have to deliver one more 25 basis point rate hike before the election and that further substantial rate increases will be necessary after the election. We continue to look for rates to rise significantly over the course of next year, probably reaching 7.5 percent by year end. The combination of sterling's appreciation and the tighter than expected budget have, however, led us to scale back our expectations of rate rises beyond this, which is a significant downward revision from the eight percent-plus rates we were looking for before sterling's meteoric rise and the budget.
SIMON BRISCOE, NIKKO EUROPE

The UK's economic outlook is barely changed by this budget...The fiscal outlook painted by the budget was more surprising. On all measures, fiscal policy is tighter than expected...It is noteworthy that the fiscal deficit will be just 2.5 percent of GDP next year, and that is a "wheeze-free" figure compared to the practices adopted in many other EU countries. The improvements compared to expectations might not be enormous but they are significant and genuine.

The politics of the budget are good -- tax cuts for all and the promise of more to come, a clamp-down on tax avoidance and spending fraud, expenditure increases on health and education and lower duty increases on most drinks. We will only see the impact in May (when the election is expected to take place), but with consumer sentiment already on the up, the chancellor has done his bit and there is nothing here to stop sentiment improving further.
The outlook for interest rates has improved fractionally.

The Chancellor clearly feels that his budget is fiscally tough and has pursued this route in order to reduce the upward pressure on base rates. Even if the Bank of England and the City feel that higher rates are required, the chancellor will need more, not less, persuading in the light of the budget that rates need to rise. He restated that he will act when he sees any risks -- he showed this only weeks ago -- but we do not expect a rate rise before the February meeting.
Gilts will receive a modest boost from the budget...The budget appears to do little to jeopardise the position of the UK equity market.
MICHAEL DICKS, LEHMAN BROTHERS

The budget feels a little of a let down...In effect, Mr Clarke has tried to adopt a prudent "middle path," no doubt believing that big tax cuts would have been viewed as a bribe to the electorate and unsustainable. Although at first blush, the budget might seem a little better for the markets than expected, because of the new PSBR forecasts and small giveaway, in fact the new measures do little to solve the economy's main problem at the moment -- the problem of rising inflation. Indeed, by including alkmost 3 bln stg of reductions in personal taxes, the budget will likely make matters worse.

The sharp acceleration in demand will continue...It is hard to imagine that RPIX will drop to 2.5 percent during the first half of next year and remain there. The Bank of England is likely to share this view. Hence, we believe that Mr George will still be asking for a rate hike as early as December. Although Mr Clarke may well refuse the move initially, we expect a rise in base rates of 25 basis points in January. Thereafter, we expect the nearness of the election to lead the Chancellor to turn down further requests for rate hikes. Once it becomes apparent to the markets that he is "behind the curve," we expect sterling to weaken.
ANDREW CATES, UBS

Given the proximity of the general election Clarke deserves some credit for avoiding the temptation to relax fiscal policy...He delivered a tight package of measures with tax cuts more than offset with public spending reductions. The budget package will therefore not add to aggregate demand in the economy. And on that score Clarke may satisfy financial markets that while monetary policy will almost certainly have to be tightened, the magnitude of the rise in interest rates that we will see next year has been reduced.

Medium-term public borrowing plans further out are still very tight. The Treasury's assumptions about how quickly the economy will grow over the next four years (at an average rate of 2.25 percent) and along with it how fast revenues will rise are too optimistic. We take issue with the government's forecast that targeted inflation will fall back to 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of next year. Cost pressures from the manufacturing sector and labour market are still pretty subdued, but we believe the strength of the domestic economy and in particular the strength of consumer demand next year will cause retailers to raise their margins.

However, we do not believe that the strength of the economy and the resulting pressures on inflation will force either a Labour or a Conservative government to raise the level of base rates to 7.0 percent.
RICHARD JEFFREY, CHARTERHOUSE

In political terms, the budget was wholly predictable. In straightforward economic terms, it provides an appreciable stimulus to consumer spending, which is already growing very fast. Even on the chancellor's own forecast, that growth is set to become unsustainably fast in 1997. Inevitably that will cause a deterioration in the trade accounts and inflation prospects.

The question is how soon that comes through. I think it is likely to be sooner than perhaps the chancellor is anticipating, therefore there will be upward pressure on interest rates for most of next year. I would have thought we would see the first increase in January, a hiatus until after the election and then rates continuing to rise towards our forecast year-end level of 8.5 percent."
ANDREW SNOWBALL, COOPERATIVE BANK
The government's spending cuts are unlikely to be met and the government in effect recognises this.

If the spending cuts cannot be met, and the pressures are likely to get worse not better as the election approaches, the overall stance of fiscal policy is likely to turn out expansionary, not restrictive. Not only can the public finances not afford this at a time when the structural PSBR is around 25 billion stg but neither can the economy. As with the balance of the tax changes, if spending overruns it will add fuel to an already overheating economy.
ROGER BOOTLE AND JONATHAN LOYNES, HSBC MARKETS

This budget was mildly contractionary, if the measures announced to reduce tax avoidance work properly and if the tight figures for public spending are adhered to. It may not have been prudent enough...to prevent the Governor of the Bank of England from pressing for further interest rate rises. The Chancellor's speech made reference to the need for monetary policy to do less of the work of containing inflation. This was a clear sign that the Treasury is geting edgy about the strength of sterling and suggests the Chancellor dearly wants to avoid further rate rises, and not only for the obvious political reasons.

But Clarke may have the ammunition to fight the Governor off. The Treasury is forecasting underlying inflation at three percent in Q4 this year and 2.5 percent in Q2 of next year. Accordingly, with sterling still strong, there remains a good chance that interest rates can be held at six percent.
The budget should...help to underpin both gilts and equities. It may also serve to weaken sterling a little. But the pound is nevertheless too well supported by the fundamentals to lose much ground."
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
